newsitem.title: USA: Jewell case prompts self-examination by U.S. press.
newsitem.headline: Jewell case prompts self-examination by U.S. press.

text.p: U.S. news organisations Monday were conducting a critical self-examination of how they turned former Olympics bombing suspect Richard Jewell from a hero into a villain without a charge or a trial.
"The press overreacted enormously," Rem Reider, editor of the American Journalism Review, said.

Howard Kurtz, media critic for the Washington Post, said the handling of the Jewell story was "a great moment of shame for the press. There's no escaping the fact that journalists ruined this guy's life on the basis of a whispered leak."

Jewell on Monday labeled "a lie" much of what was written about him before he was cleared in the July 27 Olympics bombing. He told a news conference, "The media said I fitted the profile of a lone bomber. That was a lie. The media said I was a frustrated police wannabe. That was lie ... It was all a lie."
Press experts agreed Jewell had received shoddy treatment.

"You can never set it right after you told the entire world that this guy was a terrible villain. There is always that taint of suspicion that stays with a person whose picture has been on page one," Kurtz said.
But no press expert was willing to predict that the same media frenzy would not happen again, given the right leak from the right unnamed source.

Jewell was the security guard who found a suspicious package containing a pipe bomb at Atlanta's Centennial Park during the summer games and tried to get people away from it before it exploded. For the first three days he was hailed as a hero, but then in a special edition of the Atlanta Journal he was named as a suspect in a 378-word story without attribution under a banner headline.

Because of the technology that spews news stories to all parts of the globe through print, broadcast and cyberspace, the allegations were flashed far and wide. Within minutes television reporters were reading the story aloud on air while camera crews and reporters descended on Jewell's home.

Live coverage beamed pictures of the FBI taking Jewell's belongings out for examination, including his mother's plastic kitchen ware and Walt Disney tapes. For almost three months, based on statements by unnamed government sources that said he fitted the "profile of a lone bomber," Jewell had to endure a press scrutiny that did all but convict him of the pipe-bomb explosion in which two people died and 111 were injured.
But on Saturday federal authorities announced they no longer believed Jewell had anything to do with the crime.

One of his attorneys, Wayne Grant, said Jewell was contemplating lawsuits against several news organisations and the government for not only making him a suspect but making it seem like he was, indeed, the bomber. "It will be a monumental task to coordinate the number of lawsuits on Richard's behalf," Grant added.

Reider said there was a real question as to whether the press should have gone with the story in the first place, but if editors decided to use it there were better ways to handle the story than banner headlines.
"I think it was a case of law enforcement leaking information and steering people to a suspect. There was no attribution and not a lot to base it on ... and the media ran wild with it," Reider said.

The American Journalism Review printed a detailed and critical account of the press's role in the case under the headline, "Going to Extremes." In the article Ron Martz, one of the Journal-Constitution reporters who wrote the story that started the frenzy, explained what happened in terms that many reporters would understand even if the public would not:
"We did not say he was guilty. We said the FBI was investigating him and that was very obvious from the fact that they were questioning him and had a search warrant for his apartment," Martz said.

"If we had got beaten, we would have been the laughing stock of the industry. We are the only newspaper in town. But since we broke the story naming the suspect it seems like a lot of people are coming back and questioning why we did it.
"There's some sour grapes. I get the sense that certain members of the media are trying to justify to bosses why they'd gotten beaten."
